title: Household Emergency Kit Without Clutter
description: Build a kit around daily needs, storage limits, and refresh habits instead of buying a giant one-size bundle.

sections.heading: Start with household rhythm
sections.body: A useful kit is built around the people in the home, the rooms where supplies fit, and the habits that make rotation happen before items are forgotten.
bullets: Group supplies by need: water, food, light, first aid, sanitation, communication, and documents.
Keep the first layer reachable from the main living area, not buried behind seasonal storage.
Use a printed inventory card so a family member can find supplies without an app.

sections.heading: Measure the kit before shopping
sections.body: Count the people, days, storage shelf depth, and container weight you can actually lift. Those numbers shape the container choice more than a giant bundle list.
bullets: Choose several small containers if one heavy tote would be hard to move.
Mark expiration months on the outside where they are visible.
Leave room for household-specific items such as glasses, pet supplies, and medication notes.

sections.heading: What to buy only after measuring
sections.body: Buy items that close a gap in the plan. A flashlight, radio, water container, or first-aid kit is easier to justify when it has a named job.
bullets: Prefer products with simple battery requirements and clear instructions.
Avoid mystery bundles where core item counts are hidden.
Store tools beside the supplies they support, such as a can opener near shelf-stable food.

title: Water Storage Planning for Real Homes
description: Estimate water by people, days, pets, heat, and storage space, then choose containers you will actually rotate.

sections.heading: Use the gallon math first
sections.body: The planning baseline is one gallon per person per day, then the plan should adjust for heat, pets, medical needs, and how often containers can be rotated.
bullets: Multiply people by days before choosing container size.
Add a pet buffer instead of assuming the human supply covers every use.
Split water across multiple locations if one closet is too warm or crowded.

sections.heading: Container fit matters
sections.body: Water is heavy, so container shape, handle design, and shelf height decide whether stored water remains practical.
bullets: Measure the shelf or floor space before buying containers.
Choose containers that can be lifted safely when full.
Keep a smaller pour container near a larger storage container if the large one is hard to handle.

sections.heading: Rotation checklist
sections.body: A water plan needs a visible refresh routine. Without a date and location system, even a good container becomes easy to ignore.
bullets: Label fill dates in large writing.
Keep containers away from fuels, cleaners, and heat sources.
Tie water checks to smoke-alarm checks or another household routine.

title: Power-Outage Lighting Plan
description: Separate room lighting, task lighting, and alerting so an outage does not depend on one flashlight.

sections.heading: Separate room light from task light
sections.body: A living room lantern, a hands-free headlamp, and a small bedside light solve different outage problems. Buying one bright item rarely covers every room well.
bullets: Place a light where people gather.
Keep a headlamp or clip light for breaker panels and under-sink work.
Give each sleeping area a small light that can be found by touch.

sections.heading: Power source planning
sections.body: Lighting becomes easier when batteries, charging cables, and lamp types are standardized. Mixing many battery types makes maintenance harder.
bullets: List each light and its battery or charging method.
Keep spare batteries in the same container as the lights.
For rechargeable lights, set a calendar reminder to top them off.

sections.heading: Alerting and visibility
sections.body: Outage lighting should also support communication and safety. A weather radio, reflective markers, and a simple flashlight can cover moments when phones are not enough.
bullets: Keep one light with the weather radio.
Store a flashlight near exterior doors.
Avoid using candles as the primary lighting plan.

title: Phone Charging During Outages
description: Plan charging around watt-hours, cables, and device priority instead of only counting ports.

sections.heading: Prioritize communication first
sections.body: During an outage, a phone is often a map, flashlight, alert receiver, and contact list. The charging plan should protect that role before powering comfort devices.
bullets: Decide which phone gets charged first if power is limited.
Keep one cable per common connector in the kit.
Use airplane mode or low-power mode when charging resources are limited.

sections.heading: Translate capacity into watt-hours
sections.body: Power banks are easier to compare by watt-hours than by only counting milliamp-hours, especially when tablets or larger devices are involved.
bullets: Write down the device battery size before choosing a bank.
Account for conversion loss rather than assuming perfect transfer.
Check USB-C Power Delivery needs for larger devices.

sections.heading: Storage and rotation
sections.body: A charged power bank is only useful if it can be found and has not been neglected for months.
bullets: Store the bank with its cable.
Recharge backup banks on a recurring household date.
Keep high-capacity batteries in carry-on luggage when flying and check current travel guidance.

title: Power Bank Size for Travel
description: Use watt-hours and device needs to choose a power bank that fits travel and everyday charging.

sections.heading: Start with the device list
sections.body: Travel charging depends on the phone, tablet, earbuds, camera, and fan you actually carry. Count devices before choosing capacity.
bullets: List each device and whether it uses USB-C, Lightning, or another cable.
Estimate how many full charges matter between wall outlets.
Keep one short cable in the same pouch as the bank.

sections.heading: Use watt-hours for boundaries
sections.body: Watt-hours help compare banks across labels and support flight packing decisions. Very large banks need extra attention before travel.
bullets: Look for a watt-hour marking or calculate from labeled capacity and voltage.
Check airline and FAA guidance before packing high-capacity batteries.
Carry batteries where required by current travel rules.

sections.heading: Choose shape by trip style
sections.body: A slim bank suits walking days, while a larger USB-C PD bank suits laptops and long layovers.
bullets: Choose pocketable shape for city travel.
Choose USB-C PD output for compatible tablets and laptops.
Avoid banks that hide input and output specifications.

title: USB-C Charger Buying Checklist
description: Match charger output, cable capability, plug shape, and device input before buying another brick.

sections.heading: Match charger to device input
sections.body: USB-C does not mean every charger behaves the same. The device label and manufacturer documentation decide the useful output level.
bullets: Check the device input requirement before buying.
Match the cable capability to the charger and device.
Use a compact multi-port charger only if the ports still meet the needed output when shared.

sections.heading: Travel shape and cord plan
sections.body: A folding plug, detachable cord, or extra outlet clearance can matter more than an extra port.
bullets: Check whether the charger blocks neighboring outlets.
Pack the cable length that fits hotel, airport, or bedside layouts.
Use one labeled pouch for charger, adapter, and cables.

sections.heading: What to skip
sections.body: Skip vague listings that do not state output modes or make compatibility unclear.
bullets: Look for clearly printed voltage and current output.
Prefer known connector standards over proprietary wording.
Do not rely on a plug adapter to change voltage for a charger not designed for it.

title: Portable Fan for Power Outages
description: Choose a fan by wattage, runtime, airflow location, and power source so it helps when the room gets warm.

sections.heading: Runtime is the core number
sections.body: A fan that feels useful for one hour may not solve a warm bedroom overnight. Convert watts and battery watt-hours before buying.
bullets: Divide battery watt-hours by fan watts for a rough runtime.
Plan for lower speed settings when silence and duration matter.
Keep a separate phone-charging reserve instead of draining every bank on airflow.

sections.heading: Airflow placement
sections.body: Small fans help most when they can sit safely near the person, not across a room.
bullets: Check clip, stand, or hanging options before buying.
Make sure cords do not cross walking paths in the dark.
Use airflow with hydration and heat-safety guidance.

sections.heading: Outage storage
sections.body: A fan belongs with its charging cable and a label showing typical runtime.
bullets: Store the cable in the same pouch.
Top off the battery during regular supply checks.
Pick controls that are easy to use in low light.

title: Tent Fan and Lantern Planning
description: Plan small comfort gear for a tent by runtime, hanging options, noise, and charging reality.

sections.heading: Comfort gear should earn its space
sections.body: Tent fans and lanterns compete with food, clothing, and shelter weight. Choose the item that solves a real sleep or visibility problem.
bullets: Prioritize quiet airflow for sleeping areas.
Use warm, low light for inside the tent and brighter task light outside.
Check hanging points before assuming a lantern or fan can be mounted.

sections.heading: Power and charging
sections.body: Camping charging is constrained by trip days, shade, cold, and connector compatibility.
bullets: Estimate nightly fan runtime before choosing battery size.
Keep a backup headlamp even if the lantern is rechargeable.
Match solar or battery connectors before the trip.

sections.heading: Packability
sections.body: A compact fan that cannot stand securely may be less useful than a slightly larger one with a stable base.
bullets: Test the fan on the ground and from a hanging point.
Pack cables in a bright pouch.
Avoid gear with tiny loose parts that are easy to lose at camp.

title: Camping Power Station Sizing
description: Estimate daily watt-hours for lights, phones, fans, and small devices before choosing a portable station.

sections.heading: Build the load list
sections.body: A power station should be sized from the actual camp loads: phones, lights, fan, camera, pump, or small medical device.
bullets: Write wattage and hours for each device.
Separate critical loads from comfort loads.
Add reserve for cold nights and cloudy days.

sections.heading: Capacity and output are different
sections.body: A station may have enough watt-hours but still lack the output port or wattage needed for a device.
bullets: Check AC, USB-C, USB-A, and DC outputs against your devices.
Look for continuous output, not only peak wording.
Keep cable adapters minimal to reduce failure points.

sections.heading: Recharge plan
sections.body: A battery with no recharge path must cover the full trip. Solar helps only when sun exposure and connectors work.
bullets: Estimate usable sun hours conservatively.
Test panel and battery together before leaving.
Keep lights on a smaller independent backup.

title: Solar Panel Match for Camping
description: Use sun hours, connector compatibility, and battery capacity to decide whether portable solar is useful for your trip.

sections.heading: Panel size starts with daily use
sections.body: A portable panel should replace a meaningful portion of daily watt-hours. Otherwise it becomes bulk without much benefit.
bullets: Calculate daily watt-hours from the camping-power tool.
Divide by usable sun hours to set a starting wattage.
Add margin for angle, shade, heat, and clouds.

sections.heading: Connector compatibility
sections.body: Many solar frustrations come from mismatched plugs and charging limits rather than from the panel itself.
bullets: Check the battery input port and voltage range.
Confirm whether an adapter cable is included.
Test the setup at home in sunlight.

sections.heading: When solar makes sense
sections.body: Solar is most helpful on multi-day trips with daylight basecamp time and open sky.
bullets: Skip it for short trips where a charged battery covers the load.
Use it for phones and lights before comfort devices.
Store the panel where it will not crack or bend during travel.

title: Air Mattress Pump Selector Guide
description: Choose between high-volume pumps, rechargeable pumps, and manual backup by pressure and nozzle needs.

sections.heading: Pressure and volume are separate
sections.body: Air mattresses need volume more than high pressure. A tire inflator can be too slow, while a high-volume pump may be wrong for tires.
bullets: Choose high airflow for mattresses and rafts.
Use a pressure-aware inflator for tires and balls.
Match nozzles to the valve before considering power source.

sections.heading: Power source fit
sections.body: Rechargeable pumps are convenient away from outlets, while wall-powered pumps suit guest rooms and planned setups.
bullets: Use USB rechargeable for camping and car storage.
Use wall power for frequent indoor setup.
Keep a manual backup for important sleep setups.

sections.heading: Storage and noise
sections.body: A pump that is easy to find and quick to use is more valuable than one with unused modes.
bullets: Store nozzles in a pouch attached to the pump.
Check whether deflate mode matters for packing.
Consider noise if inflating late at night.

title: Pool Float and Inflatable Pump Guide
description: Avoid overbuying by matching nozzle style, deflate mode, and recharge method to seasonal inflatables.

sections.heading: Seasonal inflatables need fast setup
sections.body: Pool floats, loungers, and toys usually need nozzle variety and deflate mode more than pressure.
bullets: Look for wide and narrow nozzle tips.
Prioritize deflate mode for storage at the end of the day.
Keep charging status visible before pool trips.

sections.heading: Avoid overinflation
sections.body: Inflatables can be damaged by forcing air after they are firm enough for their intended use.
bullets: Use short bursts near the end.
Let warmed material expand before adding more air.
Do not use tire-pressure targets for soft inflatables.

sections.heading: Storage kit
sections.body: A small seasonal pouch prevents lost nozzles and dead batteries.
bullets: Store pump, nozzles, patch kit, and charging cable together.
Label the pouch by season.
Keep the pump dry and away from pool chemicals.

title: Vehicle Tire Inflator Checklist
description: A practical checklist for matching a tire inflator to your vehicle, outlet, pressure target, and storage spot.

sections.heading: Start at the door placard
sections.body: The vehicle placard is the planning pressure reference. The number on the tire sidewall is not the routine fill target.
bullets: Write the placard PSI in the glove box notes.
Check pressure when tires are cold when practical.
Use a separate gauge to confirm readings.

sections.heading: Match duty cycle to vehicle size
sections.body: A compact car top-off and a truck tire refill are different jobs. Heat management and hose reach matter.
bullets: Check cord length from outlet to each tire.
Pause during long fills if the unit instructions require it.
Choose a storage case that keeps the hose from kinking.

sections.heading: Kit pairing
sections.body: An inflator works better as part of a small tire-care kit.
bullets: Pair it with a gauge and valve caps.
Keep gloves and a light nearby.
Store it where luggage will not crush the hose.

title: Tire Pressure Gauge Basics
description: Understand why a simple gauge belongs beside any inflator and how it fits tire-care routines.

sections.heading: Why the gauge still matters
sections.body: Built-in inflator displays are useful, but a separate gauge gives an independent check and can live in the vehicle full time.
bullets: Use the gauge before and after filling.
Compare readings occasionally to catch drift.
Choose a display you can read in daylight and low light.

sections.heading: Analog or digital
sections.body: Either style can work if it is easy to use and stored correctly.
bullets: Analog gauges avoid battery maintenance.
Digital gauges can be easier to read quickly.
Protect the gauge from dirt and heavy impact.

sections.heading: Routine placement
sections.body: The gauge should live where tire checks happen, not in a drawer at home.
bullets: Keep it with the inflator or in the door pocket.
Add valve caps to the same pouch.
Record the vehicle placard pressure on a label.

title: Car Emergency Kit for Commuters
description: Build a compact kit for local commuting without turning the trunk into a storage locker.

sections.heading: Design for short disruptions
sections.body: A commuter kit should handle a flat tire, dead phone, dark parking lot, minor injury, and traffic delay without filling the trunk.
bullets: Use a small bin or seat-back pouch.
Prioritize visibility, light, water, first aid, and phone power.
Keep work shoes or weather layers in mind if you commute dressed for indoors.

sections.heading: Water and comfort
sections.body: A short commute can become a long wait when roads close. Water and warmth or cooling are compact safeguards.
bullets: Add water that can be rotated easily.
Include a compact blanket or cooling cloth based on climate.
Keep snacks separate from fluids to reduce mess.

sections.heading: Finding items quickly
sections.body: The kit should be reachable from the driver area or trunk edge.
bullets: Use clear pouches by category.
Place a light at the top.
Review the kit after seasonal changes.

title: Cold Weather Car Kit
description: Prioritize warmth, visibility, traction, and communication for winter driving disruptions.

sections.heading: Warmth before convenience
sections.body: Cold-weather kits should help a person stay visible, warm, and able to communicate during a delay.
bullets: Add gloves, hat, blanket, and extra socks.
Include a scraper and traction aid if conditions call for it.
Keep phone power and charging cable in the vehicle.

sections.heading: Visibility in snow and dark
sections.body: Winter delays often combine poor light with poor road visibility.
bullets: Use reflective markers or a vest.
Keep a headlamp accessible.
Store batteries where cold exposure is considered.

sections.heading: Water and food choices
sections.body: Choose items that tolerate vehicle temperature swings and are easy to rotate.
bullets: Use water containers that can handle freezing expansion space.
Choose snacks that do not melt or crumble easily.
Check the kit after severe weather passes.

title: Hot Weather Car Kit
description: Plan water, shade, cooling, and phone power for summer roadside delays.

sections.heading: Heat changes priorities
sections.body: Hot-weather kits should emphasize water, shade, cooling, and communication while avoiding supplies that degrade in a hot cabin.
bullets: Store water where it can be rotated often.
Add a sunshade, cooling cloth, and hat.
Keep phone power out of direct sun when possible.

sections.heading: Roadside delay planning
sections.body: A summer breakdown can become uncomfortable quickly, especially with children, pets, or medical needs.
bullets: Plan extra water for passengers and pets.
Keep a small towel or cloth for shade and grip.
Do not leave people or pets in a hot parked vehicle.

sections.heading: Product checks
sections.body: Heat can affect adhesives, batteries, and soft materials.
bullets: Inspect stored items after heat waves.
Use a case that keeps tools organized.
Replace warped or leaking supplies immediately.

title: Carry-On Luggage Measurement Guide
description: Measure the real exterior of a packed bag and leave room for airline-specific rules.

sections.heading: Measure the real exterior
sections.body: Carry-on planning starts with the packed bag, including wheels, handles, and outside pockets.
bullets: Measure length, width, and height after packing.
Use the luggage-size tool to calculate linear inches.
Leave margin because airline sizers and rules differ.

sections.heading: Weight is a separate issue
sections.body: A bag can fit the sizer and still be hard to lift or restricted by an airline weight rule.
bullets: Use a luggage scale before leaving home.
Move dense items into a personal item only if rules allow it.
Keep medicines and essentials accessible.

sections.heading: Bag features that help
sections.body: The useful features are the ones that make measurement and inspection easier.
bullets: Look for published exterior dimensions.
Choose handles that do not protrude awkwardly.
Use packing cubes to keep security checks tidy.

title: Packing Cubes vs Compression Bags
description: Pick organization tools by clothing type, inspection access, and whether compression creates a weight problem.

sections.heading: Organization and compression differ
sections.body: Packing cubes sort items. Compression bags reduce volume but can create dense, awkward bundles.
bullets: Use cubes for shirts, underwear, socks, and categories.
Use compression for bulky soft items only when weight is controlled.
Keep liquids and electronics separate for inspection.

sections.heading: Access during travel
sections.body: The right organizer depends on whether you unpack once or live out of the bag.
bullets: Choose cubes for multi-stop trips.
Use transparent or mesh tops to identify contents.
Avoid over-compressing items needed on travel day.

sections.heading: Fit check
sections.body: Organizers should match the bag interior instead of creating unused corners.
bullets: Measure the suitcase interior.
Use fewer larger cubes for checked bags and smaller cubes for carry-ons.
Test the packed bag with the luggage-size checker.

title: Travel Adapter vs Voltage Converter
description: Separate plug-shape problems from voltage problems before plugging in a device overseas.

sections.heading: Plug shape is not voltage
sections.body: An adapter changes the physical plug interface. A converter addresses voltage for devices that are not compatible with the destination supply.
bullets: Read the device label for input voltage.
Use IEC plug references to identify destination plug type.
Do not assume a universal adapter changes voltage.

sections.heading: Dual-voltage devices
sections.body: Many modern chargers are dual voltage, but heat tools and appliances often need closer checking.
bullets: Look for 100-240V wording on the device or charger.
Check grounded plug needs separately.
Pack a USB charger that matches device charging requirements.

sections.heading: Safer travel kit
sections.body: A small labeled kit prevents wrong-cable surprises at the hotel.
bullets: Pack adapter, charger, and cable together.
Use a grounded adapter when the device needs ground.
Leave questionable appliances at home rather than guessing.

title: International USB Charging Kit
description: Build a simple USB charging kit that covers plugs, cables, power banks, and device labels.

sections.heading: Build around USB first
sections.body: Phones, earbuds, e-readers, and tablets can often share a compact USB charging kit when cables are planned.
bullets: List every connector before packing.
Use one multi-port charger only if shared output still meets needs.
Include a short cable and a longer bedside cable.

sections.heading: Destination plug planning
sections.body: The wall interface depends on country plug type, while the device side depends on USB standards.
bullets: Use a plug adapter for the destination.
Check whether your charger is dual voltage.
Keep spare cables away from liquids and toiletries.

sections.heading: Battery travel notes
sections.body: Power banks add flexibility but need travel-rule attention.
bullets: Check watt-hour marking before flights.
Carry batteries according to current aviation guidance.
Keep the power bank accessible for screening if needed.

title: Small Apartment Emergency Storage
description: Use compact containers, vertical space, and modular categories for preparedness in limited storage.

sections.heading: Use vertical and modular storage
sections.body: Small homes need emergency supplies that fit normal life. Narrow bins, under-bed boxes, and door shelves can work better than one large tote.
bullets: Map three storage zones: water, food, and tools.
Use clear containers so supplies can be checked quickly.
Avoid blocking exits or electrical panels.

sections.heading: Break the kit into categories
sections.body: Distributed storage is easier when every container has a theme and label.
bullets: Keep first aid and light near the main living area.
Store water where weight is supported.
Place documents in a grab-and-go pouch.

sections.heading: Refresh without clutter
sections.body: Small spaces punish forgotten supplies, so rotation needs to be simple.
bullets: Use household foods that can be rotated into normal meals.
Check labels during rent, insurance, or seasonal paperwork.
Donate or use duplicate items before adding new ones.

title: Family Emergency Supply Refresh Routine
description: Make supplies easier to rotate by tying dates, labels, and locations to normal household habits.

sections.heading: Make refresh dates visible
sections.body: A family kit stays useful when someone can see what needs attention without opening every container.
bullets: Put a month label on each bin.
Keep a one-page inventory in the top container.
Assign categories rather than asking one person to remember everything.

sections.heading: Tie checks to existing habits
sections.body: The easiest refresh routine attaches to something already happening at home.
bullets: Check batteries when clocks change if that routine fits your household.
Review water and food before storm season or travel season.
Update contact cards after school, work, or medical changes.

sections.heading: Reduce friction
sections.body: Small replacements are easier than rebuilding a neglected kit.
bullets: Keep a shopping note for only missing categories.
Use containers that are easy to open and close.
Store instruction manuals in a single folder.

title: Pet-Friendly Emergency Kit
description: Add pet food, water, leash, carrier, sanitation, and comfort items to the household planning math.

sections.heading: Add pets to the math
sections.body: Pet planning affects water, food, sanitation, transport, and comfort. It should not be an afterthought in the household kit.
bullets: Add water and food by pet and day.
Keep a leash, carrier, or restraint where it can be reached quickly.
Store copies of vaccination and microchip information.

sections.heading: Sanitation and comfort
sections.body: Pet supplies can prevent stress and mess during an evacuation or outage.
bullets: Pack waste bags, litter needs, and cleaning wipes.
Include a familiar small blanket or toy if space allows.
Keep medication instructions with the pet documents.

sections.heading: Buying checklist
sections.body: Choose pet kit containers that are easy to carry with human supplies.
bullets: Use waterproof labels.
Separate food from cleaning products.
Refresh pet food before normal feeding routines change.

title: Food Safety During Power Outages
description: Choose thermometers, coolers, and power priorities that support safer food decisions during an outage.

sections.heading: Temperature decides the plan
sections.body: Food-safety decisions during an outage depend on time, temperature, and whether cold storage stayed closed.
bullets: Use appliance thermometers in refrigerator and freezer spaces.
Keep a cooler plan for essential items.
Open cold storage only when needed.

sections.heading: Power priorities
sections.body: Not every appliance can or should be powered by a small battery. Decide what must stay cold before an outage.
bullets: Prioritize medical refrigeration if applicable.
Use generators only with proper outdoor placement and safety guidance.
Keep phone alerts and radio updates separate from food decisions.

sections.heading: Supplies that help decisions
sections.body: Thermometers, coolers, ice packs, and labels support safer choices without guesswork.
bullets: Freeze water containers ahead of storms when possible.
Label cooler contents by priority.
Keep food-safety source guidance with the emergency folder.

title: Smoke Alarm and Battery Checks
description: Turn alarm checks, batteries, and reminders into a simple home-safety rhythm.

sections.heading: Alarms need a routine
sections.body: Smoke alarms are easy to ignore until they chirp. A written routine keeps testing, battery checks, and replacement planning visible.
bullets: List alarm locations by room.
Test according to current safety guidance.
Keep spare batteries only for alarms that use replaceable batteries.

sections.heading: Match batteries correctly
sections.body: Wrong or weak batteries create nuisance issues and reduce trust in the alarm system.
bullets: Use the battery type specified by the alarm.
Label the install month where appropriate.
Replace alarms according to manufacturer and safety guidance.

sections.heading: Connect to the emergency kit
sections.body: Alarm checks are a natural moment to inspect flashlights and other household safety supplies.
bullets: Check lights and radio at the same time.
Update the emergency contact card.
Clear clutter around exits while doing the walk-through.

title: Portable Generator Safety Boundaries
description: Keep generator planning focused on outdoor placement, carbon monoxide risk, cords, and load discipline.

sections.heading: Safety boundaries come first
sections.body: Generator planning starts with carbon monoxide risk, outdoor placement, extension cords, and load discipline before convenience.
bullets: Keep generators outdoors and away from openings according to safety guidance.
Use carbon monoxide alarms in the home.
Never treat a garage as a safe operating space.

sections.heading: Load planning
sections.body: A generator should power selected essentials, not every device in the house.
bullets: List critical loads before buying accessories.
Use cords rated for the intended load and environment.
Keep fuel storage away from living areas and ignition sources.

sections.heading: Outage workflow
sections.body: A written sequence reduces mistakes when the lights are already out.
bullets: Post setup steps with the generator supplies.
Store flashlights so setup does not happen in darkness.
Review safety guidance before storm season.
